e.etymology: An American variant of Gerald, from Germanic ger, 'spear', and wald, 'rule', with a spelling that leans on Harold.
From the surname Cloyd. As a first name it sits close to Clyde and Floyd, which were popular in the same years.

A Japanese girls' name ending in ko, 'child'. The first part depends on the characters chosen, often tami, 'people', or ta and mi, 'much beauty'. The 1962 film A Girl Named Tamiko brought it to the US.
A feminine elaboration of Verna or Vernon with the -etta ending, used in the US in the early 1900s.
A phonetic spelling of Beulah, from Hebrew be'ulah, 'married'. In Isaiah 62 it is a name for the restored land of Israel, and Beulah Land became an image of heaven in English hymns.
An American name of the 1970s that puts the Sh- sound on Sandra, or respells Chandra, an Indian name from Sanskrit chandra, 'moon'.
A respelling of Melissa, the Greek word for honeybee, from meli, 'honey'. In Greek myth Melissa was a nymph who cared for the infant Zeus.

A Swedish and Finnish name from the 1800s, probably a form of Helma, the short form of Wilhelmina, or a feminine of Hilmar. Scandinavian immigrants brought it to the US; the painter Hilma af Klint bore it.
A respelling of Debbie, the pet form of Deborah, Hebrew for 'bee'. In the Bible Deborah is a prophetess and judge of Israel.
The German form of Gerald, from Germanic ger, 'spear', and wald, 'rule'. In the US it mostly served as a spelling of Gerald.
From the English word earth with a feminine -a, in use in the US since the late 1800s. Singer and actress Eartha Kitt made it famous.
namesakes: Eartha Kitt (singer and actress, Santa Baby, Catwoman)

assoc.t: Eartha Kitt, singer of Santa Baby and TV's Catwoman

e.etymology: A phonetic American spelling of Siobhan, the Irish form of Joan, from Hebrew Yochanan, 'God is gracious'. The -onne ending follows Yvonne.
A joining of Dee and Ann, and a spelling of Deanne, which is a form of Diane or a feminine of Dean.
A spelling of Shawna or Shauna, the feminine of Shaun, an English spelling of Sean, the Irish form of John. John comes from Hebrew Yochanan, 'God is gracious'.
A feminine form of Will or William with the -ene ending, used in the American South in the 1920s and 30s. William comes from Germanic wil, 'will', and helm, 'helmet, protection'.
A respelling of Megan, a Welsh pet form of Meg, short for Margaret, from Greek margarites, 'pearl'.
A phonetic spelling of Bernice, from Berenike, the Macedonian form of Greek Pherenike, 'bringer of victory'. This spelling was given to boys as well as girls in the early 1900s.

For girls, a spelling of Nicole, the French feminine of Nicholas, from Greek nike, 'victory', and laos, 'people'. Nichol is also a medieval English form of Nicholas that survives as a Scottish surname.
The everyday medieval English form of Agnes, which was said without the g. Agnes comes from Greek hagne, 'pure, chaste'. Annis lasted as a first name and a surname.
An English surname from places named with Old English north and wudu, 'wood'.
A joining of Rose and Ann, and a spelling of Roseanne. Rose is the flower, from Latin rosa, and Ann comes from Hebrew Channah, 'grace'.
A respelling of Jennifer, the Cornish form of Guinevere, from Welsh Gwenhwyfar. The first part is gwen, 'white, fair'; the second is often read as 'smooth' or 'phantom'.
A Scottish surname from the office of door-ward, the keeper of the king's door (Old English duru and weard). Walter Scott's 1823 novel Quentin Durward made it known as a first name.
An American name of the 1960s and 70s, a variant of Tamela and Tamara in the family of Tammy names.

A spelling of Doreen, an English and Irish name of the late 1800s that adds the -een ending to Dora or Dorothy (Greek doron, 'gift'). Dorine is also French, as in the sharp-tongued maid of Molière's Tartuffe.
A spelling of Shawna, the feminine of Shawn, an English spelling of Sean, the Irish form of John. John comes from Hebrew Yochanan, 'God is gracious'.
An African American name of the 1970s that joins the Sha- prefix to Wanda.
A spelling of Merle, from French merle, 'blackbird' (Latin merula). Merle became a first name in the US in the late 1800s for both boys and girls.
A respelling of Becky, the pet form of Rebecca, from Hebrew Rivqah, the wife of Isaac in Genesis. The Hebrew name may come from a root meaning 'to tie' or 'to join'.
e.note: Becky is current slang for a stereotypically basic or entitled white woman.

e.etymology: From an English surname, usually a form of Wyman, from the Old English name Wigmund, joining wig, 'battle', and mund, 'protection'.
